To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the brain of the preterm infant has a unique developmental trajectory and is vulnerable to injury at any stage of development.

preterm birth is associated with an increase in the incidence and prevalence of cerebral palsy and other motor disorders in the first 2–3 years of life, and that the severity of cerebral palsy is strongly associated with the severity of brain injury in preterm birth.
the brain of the premature infant is vulnerable to a wide range of insults and that the resulting brain injuries are often associated with axonal and neuronal abnormalities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new and more effective treatments of brain injury in premature infants.
the neuroanatomy of preterm brain and the neuroanatomic basis for the encephalopathy and neurodevelopmental disorders that are associated with preterm birth.
the development of a new generation of materials that can be used as an alternative to the traditional materials currently used for the treatment of bone defects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the neuroanatomical changes of prematurity are a result of a combination of factors including: (1) the immaturity of the brain and its blood supply, (2) the presence of hypoxia and hypotension, and (3) the use of therapeutic interventions.
the brain of the premature newborn is immature and that the brain of a newborn of 30–34 weeks of gestation is more immature than that of a newborn of more than 35 weeks of gestation.
the brain of the premature infant at birth is not mature, but that the brain of a 24 week gestation infant is more immature than the brain of a term infant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the preterm infant brain is not a miniature of the term infant brain.

the brain of preterm infants, especially those with very low birth weight, is not mature enough to handle the stresses of extrauterine life, and that these stresses result in a cascade of events that can lead to injury and encephalopathy.
the brain of the preterm infant has a high capacity to adapt to injury.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to be more aware of what we are doing when we are doing it.
the preterm brain has an inherent vulnerability to injury, which is related to its maturational stage at the time of injury and to the type of injury sustained.
the preterm brain is not simply an immature brain, but a unique brain that is different from both the full-term and postnatal brain.
